title: 使役形 させる — the causative: make/let someone do

grammarPoints.rule: The causative makes/lets someone else do something. For a godan (u-verb), bend the dictionary form's final -u sound back to its -a partner — the same naiStem you already use for ない and volitional — then add せる: よむ → よま + せる = よませる, 'make/let (someone) read.' かく → かかせる, はなす → はなさせる, かえる → かえらせる — every godan verb follows this one move. The MEANING (make vs let) is never in the verb itself — it rides the particle marking the person caused to act, covered next lesson.

examples.ja: はなす → はなさせる
かえる → かえらせる

antiPattern.why: せる only glues onto a verb stem that already ends in -a — an u-verb has to bend FIRST: よむ → よま, then + せる. よませる, never よむせる.

grammarPoints.rule: An ichidan (ru-verb) does what it always does — drop る, add the ending whole: たべる → たべ + させる = たべさせる, 'make/let (someone) eat.' みる → みさせる follows the same move. The two irregulars are two words to memorize outright: する → させる, くる → こさせる. Notice godan せる and ichidan させる are close cousins — both are 'the verb, plus something-seru' — but only ichidan (and both irregulars) get the extra さ.

examples.ja: たべる → たべさせる

antiPattern.why: an ichidan verb needs the FULL させる ending, not just せる — たべ+させる. Dropping the さ is a godan move borrowed onto the wrong class.

grammarPoints.rule: The causative verb never tells you MAKE vs LET by itself — the PARTICLE marking the person caused to act does, and for an intransitive verb (jidoushi — you already own this family from m33/m41) you get a real choice: を marks them as being MADE/FORCED, に marks them as being LET/PERMITTED. こどもを あるかせた, 'made the child walk' (forced) — こどもに あるかせた, 'let the child walk' (permitted) — same verb あるかせた, opposite reading, only the particle moves. This works because あるく never had its own を to begin with (it's intransitive), so を is free to be repurposed as the forced-causee marker.

examples.ja: おやは こどもを あるかせた。
examples.en: The parent made the child walk.

examples.ja: おやは こどもに あるかせた。
examples.en: The parent let the child walk.

examples.ja: せんせいは がくせいを あるかせた。
examples.en: The teacher made the student walk.

antiPattern.ja: おやは むりやり こどもに あるかせた。
antiPattern.why: むりやり ('forcibly') signals that the child was MADE to walk — but に marks the causee as being LET, not forced, and those two signals contradict each other. The forced reading needs を instead: おやは むりやり こどもを あるかせた。

grammarPoints.rule: A TRANSITIVE verb (tadoushi) already owns を for its own direct object, so the causee can only take に — こどもに やさいを たべさせる, 'made/let the child eat vegetables,' never こどもを やさいを (two を in one clause is never legal). With を unavailable, MAKE vs LET has to be read from CONTEXT and adverbs instead of the particle: むりやり ('forcibly') signals the MADE reading unambiguously — おやは こどもに むりやり いぬを そだてさせる, 'forcibly made the child raise the dog.' Drop むりやり and the same そだてさせる leans toward the neutral/LET reading instead.

examples.ja: おやは こどもに むりやり いぬを そだてさせる。
examples.en: The parent forcibly makes the child raise the dog.

examples.ja: おやは こどもに いぬを そだてさせる。
examples.en: The parent lets the child raise the dog.

examples.ja: おやは こどもに むりやり やさいを たべさせる。
examples.en: The parent forcibly makes the child eat vegetables.

antiPattern.ja: おやは こどもを いぬを そだてさせる。
antiPattern.why: a transitive verb's causee can never take を — いぬ already has it. The causee always takes に with a transitive causative: こどもに いぬを そだてさせる。

grammarPoints.rule: Two everyday requests both ride the causative's て-form. させて ください asks permission to do something YOURSELF — しゅくだいを させて ください, 'please let me do the homework.' させて もらう describes RECEIVING that permission, riding the favor-ladder (m35) you already own — せんせいに しゅくだいを させて もらう, 'I get to do the homework (thanks to the teacher letting me).' Both are humble, self-directed requests — never confuse them with ordering someone ELSE to do something, which stays plain させる with no て-chain.

examples.ja: しゅくだいを させて ください。
examples.en: Please let me do the homework.

examples.ja: かえらせて ください。
せんせいに しゅくだいを させて もらう。
examples.en: I get to do the homework (with the teacher's permission).

antiPattern.ja: しゅくだいを させて くれる。
antiPattern.why: させて くれる would mean someone ELSE offered without being asked — a different rung of the same favor-ladder. Asking permission for yourself needs させて ください (the request) or させて もらう (describing that you received it), never くれる.

grammarPoints.rule: One more shape to RECOGNIZE, not produce yet: させて いただく. It is させて もらう's own ultra-polite twin, built from causative-te plus the humble receiving verb いただく you already met (m31, recognition only there too) — しゅくだいを させて いただく, 'I humbly get to do the homework.' You will hear this constantly in formal Japanese (especially from someone about to do something, asking implicit permission first), but production — and its trickier cousin, the causative-PASSIVE させられる — waits until n4-21, where humble language gets its own full module.

examples.ja: しゅくだいを させて いただく。
examples.en: I humbly get to do the homework.

examples.ja: しつもんを させて いただいた。
examples.en: I humbly got to ask a question.

antiPattern.ja: しゅくだいを させられる。
antiPattern.why: させられる is the CAUSATIVE-PASSIVE — 'I am made to do the homework' (unwillingly) — a completely different, much later shape (n4-21). させて いただく is a humble, WILLING request-and-receive; never confuse the two just because both start with させ.

beats.stem: しゅくだいを させて
beats.en: Please let me do the homework.
beats.explanation: させて ください is the direct request form — 'please let me.' させて もらう describes RECEIVING permission (a different sentence shape); させて くれる would mean someone offered without being asked.

beats.stem: おやは こどもに しゅくだいを

beats.explanation: しゅくだいを させる pairs する's causative with しゅくだい — よませる is よむ's causative (wrong verb), たべさせる is たべる's (also wrong verb).
